name: PT Merdeka Battery Materials Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Merdeka Battery Materials: the ore reset is real, the equity already pays for it
frontmatter.summary: REDUCE with a Rp245 target, -21.4% against the Rp312 price. The revised ore benchmark did reset Merdeka's mining margin, but the royalty is charged on the new ore price, the limonite reserve ends the mine inside two decades, and the smelter minorities rank ahead of the listed shareholder.
thesis: The Mineral Benchmark Price revisions of 15 April and 15 September 2026 are real and already delivered: 3Q26 limonite realised US$24.2/wmt per wet tonne against US$15.3/wmt in FY2025, and the mine is now the group's profit centre [S3][S2].

The royalty follows the ore price, not group revenue: US$5.3/wmt per wet tonne on limonite and US$9.4/wmt on saprolite in 3Q26, a charge of 9.3% of consolidated revenue against the 52.7 USD m of royalties charged in FY2025 on revenue of 1,435 USD m [S3][S2].

Costs are at the last actual, not at the last good year: limonite cash cost was US$12.3/wmt per wet tonne in 3Q26 against US$10.0/wmt in FY2025, and guidance below the old level is no longer being met [S3].

The life-of-asset DCF now stops where the ore stops, at 182,400 kt wmt of proven and 255,300 kt wmt of probable limonite, so the model no longer credits the equity with seven years of ore that does not exist [S2].
The mine is held indirectly and only half-owned, and minorities take 70.6% of net profit, so the consolidated cash flows this DCF produces are not the listed shareholder's [S2][S0].

catalysts.event: Extraordinary general meeting to approve the private placement of up to {{fact.F23|num0}} new shares and a paid-in capital increase of about {{in.share_change.FY2027E|pct}}.
Full-year 2026 results and 2027 guidance: the first clean read on the revised ore benchmark, on the royalty actually paid and on limonite sales at the top of the guided range.

blocks.text: We move Merdeka Battery Materials to REDUCE with a Rp245 target, -21.4% against the Rp312 price, reversing the initiation. The change is not a view on nickel: the house metals deck is unchanged, with the benchmark rising from 17,089.2 USD/t in FY2026E to 17,500.0 USD/t in FY2027E. The change is that the ore reset, which the initiation was right to identify, is now charged against the equity at the rates the company actually pays [S3].

Four corrections do the work, and each is sourced. The royalty is levied on ore value, not on group revenue: 3Q26 limonite royalty was US$5.3/wmt per wet tonne and saprolite US$9.4/wmt, a charge equal to 9.3% of consolidated revenue against the 52.7 USD m of royalties charged in FY2025 on revenue of 1,435 USD m [S3][S2]. Costs are at the last actual: limonite cash cost was US$12.3/wmt per wet tonne in 3Q26 against US$10.0/wmt in FY2025 [S3]. The DCF ends at limonite depletion rather than at a round horizon, drawing 182,400 kt wmt proven plus 255,300 kt wmt probable over the life of the mine [S2]. And the revenue per tonne of limonite tapers, because processing revenue is guided flat while ore revenue scales with volume [S3].
The result is a value far below the price. The life-of-asset DCF is worth Rp39 per share on the base case, an enterprise value of US$1,614.5m before the bridge in

, which deducts net debt at the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and book non-controlling interests, and adds associates and the placement item [S0][S7]. The base case is worth Rp46 rolled forward twelve months, the bear case Rp0 and the bull case Rp889. The equity is a levered call on the ore price: with the operating cost base fixed per tonne, a tenth on the realised ore price moves the equity value by several times that, which is why the probability-weighted target sits above the base case and why the rating is REDUCE rather than a stronger sell [S3].

What the market is paying for is the old economics. At today's price the enterprise is capitalised well above the life-of-asset DCF, which is what the ore margin looked like before the royalty and the cost base were read at their actual rates. Our call is that the revised formula now shows in the P&L at both ends of it: the mine receives a higher price and pays a higher royalty, and the smelters pay the same higher price for feed, which is why the processing lines went to a negative cash margin in the third quarter [S3].

Merdeka Battery Materials is the nickel platform of the Merdeka group and operates an integrated chain from a laterite mine in Sulawesi through rotary-kiln electric furnaces to nickel pig iron, through a matte smelter, and increasingly through high-pressure acid leach circuits that will make battery-grade mixed hydroxide precipitate. The company reports in US dollars and sells four physical products: limonite ore, saprolite ore, nickel in NPI, and nickel in high-grade matte, with sulphuric acid from the Acid Iron Metal plant as a fifth and fast-growing line [S2].

The mine is the SCM concession. At the end of 2025 it carried limonite reserves of 182,400 kt wmt proven and 255,300 kt wmt probable, and saprolite reserves of 34,500 kt wmt and 106,700 kt wmt at the same date, the limonite at a grade a shade above one and a quarter per cent nickel [S2]. Those two statements are what set the life of the asset in this report, and they are kept separate because the total ore reserve line of 578,800 kt wmt sums both ore types and cannot size a limonite DCF [S2]. FY2025 output was 14.7 million wmt of limonite against 16,800 thousand wet tonnes sold, with 73,871 t Ni produced in nickel pig iron and LGNM and a further 19,998 t Ni in matte, which is the mix the FY2025 accounts consolidate [S2].

The third quarter of 2026 is the best current description of the business. The mine produced 9.0 million wmt of limonite and sold 7.6 million wmt, so it built stock rather than drawing it down, and the great majority of saprolite deliveries went to the group's own furnaces and were eliminated on consolidation [S3]. A production record is therefore not a sales record, and it is sales that the revenue line follows. Nickel in NPI was produced at a rate above the FY2025 quarterly average and nickel in matte below it, and the acid plant ran at nameplate [S3].

The strategy is vertical integration into the battery chain rather than further mining growth. The company is ramping the PT ESG high-pressure acid leach lines, which reached near-full capacity utilisation by the end of the third quarter with mixed hydroxide precipitate output in the low tens of thousands of tonnes on an annualised basis, and it has obtained the industrial licence for the SLNC plant with first production targeted this year [S3]. A previous placement funded a feed-preparation plant and an acid-leach circuit sized in the tens of thousands of tonnes of precipitate a year, and the current placement is presented as capital strengthening for the same chain [S7].

Ownership is concentrated. The controlling shareholder holds half the register, the public holds roughly a third and two industrial holders sit above the disclosure threshold, leaving a free float of 26.5% on the exchange definition [S2][S0]. The shares trade on the Indonesia Stock Exchange with average daily value traded of IDR59.6bn, which is deep enough that the house liquidity ladder applies no discount [S0]. The structural point is that the SCM mine is held indirectly and only half-owned, and the smelters are partly owned too, so a large share of the consolidated cash flow the DCF produces belongs to minorities rather than to the listed shareholder [S2].

Revenue mix has shifted toward ore. In the third quarter the ore lines were the largest single contributor to the sales table, ahead of nickel in NPI and nickel in matte, and acid added a further block that did not exist at this scale a year earlier [S3]. That mix is why we model the company on a revenue-per-tonne-of-limonite basis rather than on smelter throughput, and why the assumption file discloses that the smelter volumes are carried inside the ratio rather than modelled separately.

Laterite nickel mining in Indonesia separates a low-grade limonite horizon, processed by high-pressure acid leach into battery-grade precipitate, from a higher-grade saprolite horizon, which is smelted in rotary kilns into nickel pig iron or further refined into matte for stainless and battery supply chains. The two routes have different capital intensity, different energy demand and different sensitivity to the government's ore benchmark, which is why an integrated operator can see margins move from the smelter to the mine within a single policy cycle.

The nickel industry's marginal cost setter is Indonesia, and Indonesian policy is therefore the industry's supply function. The country's ore benchmark, the Harga Patokan Mineral, is a government reference used for royalty and tax assessment; the 2025 annual report describes a market in which Indonesian supply growth had pushed prices down through the year, and this company's revenue fell with them [S2]. The revisions of 15 April and 15 September 2026 changed the formula, and the company's own words are that the September revision brings limonite benchmark prices closer to prevailing market prices and is expected to narrow the gap between realised selling prices and the reference used for royalty and tax [S3].

The consequence is visible in the third-quarter margins, and it cuts both ways. Saprolite realised price rose to US$66.8/wmt per wet tonne and limonite to US$24.2/wmt, and the company describes the driver explicitly as the revised benchmark framework [S3]. The same revision raised what the mine pays: royalty was US$9.4/wmt per wet tonne on saprolite and US$5.3/wmt on limonite, and the smelters now buy feed at the new reference, which is why nickel pig iron cash cost printed at US$13,886/t Ni and the matte line went to a negative cash margin [S3]. This is a regulatory re-pricing of the ore, not a market rally in nickel: the London benchmark the model carries was roughly flat through the comparison, and the processing margin squeeze is the mirror image of the mining gain [S3].

Competitive position rests on integration and on grade rather than on scale alone. Merdeka sits inside the Morowali industrial park, sells limonite to neighbouring high-pressure acid leach customers as well as to its own circuits, and converts saprolite in its own furnaces, so it captures the ore margin internally when prices rise and is exposed to the conversion margin when they fall [S3]. The reserve grade of just over one and a quarter per cent nickel and the reserve life give it a cost position that does not depend on a single year's stripping, but that life is finite and it is the constraint the valuation now models [S2].

The permitting regime is the supply lever on both sides of the trade. The company's 2026 targets are explicitly subject to RKAB approval, and no archived source states the approved tonnage for 2026 or for 2027 [S2]. The government has said publicly that it is preparing production restrictions through RKAB to support prices [S4]. We therefore carry the guided volume only up to the reserve and disclose that the permitted tonnage beyond the current year is unverified.

The moat is moderate and policy-dependent. A buyer of limonite in the park has few alternative nearby suppliers and the ore is not substitutable in the short run, which supports the realised price; but the same buyer can build its own acid-leach capacity, and the government can change the benchmark again [S3]. We therefore treat the current ore margin as the base case because it is the company's executed reality, and carry a policy reversal inside the bear case rather than in the base.

Demand-side exposure is split. Nickel pig iron and matte feed stainless and battery supply chains, and the acid plant sells into the same park's leach circuits, so the company's fortunes are tied to Indonesian processing capacity utilisation rather than to a single end market [S3]. The practical competitive question is not whether nickel demand grows but whether Indonesian ore supply stays disciplined; a quota-driven tightening lifts the price that both the ore and the smelter lines realise.

The five-forces picture is unfavourable on rivalry and favourable on supplier power. Rivalry among Indonesian integrated producers is intense and capacity has been added faster than demand, which is the reason prices fell through 2025 [S2]. Supplier power sits with the government as licensor and benchmark setter; buyer power is concentrated in a handful of park customers; the threat of substitutes is low for nickel in stainless and rising only slowly in batteries; and new entry requires a reserve, a licence and capital, which limits it but does not stop it [S3].

External influences are three. The nickel price deck drives roughly the whole revenue line through the realisation ratio; fuel sets the mining cost through the coal deck link; and the rupiah affects the debt stack, which is partly IDR-denominated even though the company reports in dollars [S3]. We hold the first two at house deck values and treat the third as a disclosed sensitivity rather than a forecast.

Revenue ran from US$1,844.7m in FY2024A down to US$1,434.5m in FY2025A, and the decomposition explains the whole move: limonite ore sales rose to 16,800 thousand wet tonnes from 11,000 thousand, while the limonite average selling price fell to US$15.3 per wet tonne from US$16.5 [S2]. Selling more ore for less money is the definition of the 2025 Indonesian ore glut, and it is why the equity de-rated before the benchmark formula was revised [S3]. The mine was working; the price was not.

The model is deliberately a single-denominator build, and the reader should hold that in mind throughout. Volume is limonite ore sold in thousand wet tonnes; the price line is total consolidated revenue divided by that tonnage. The company's own mine-gate limonite price of US$15.3/wmt and the model's US$122.7 per wet tonne are therefore not the same quantity, and the difference is the revenue from nickel in NPI, nickel in matte, saprolite and acid, which is carried inside the ratio rather than modelled stream by stream [S2][S3]. The cost line of US$85.7 per wet tonne is built the same way, from a mining cost of US$12.3 per bank cubic metre at a strip ratio of 1.0, a fuel term tied to the coal deck at a 30.0% share, a royalty of 9.3% of revenue, and a residual block of US$71.4 per wet tonne that carries processing, smelting and overhead [S2]. We disclose the abstraction rather than hide it because it is the main reason our revenue line differs from a mine-gate calculation.

The revenue ratio tapers for the same reason in reverse. Processing revenue is guided flat at the current nickel pig iron and high-grade matte ranges, so as limonite sales rise toward the top of the guided range the flat block is spread over more tonnes and revenue per wet tonne falls: US$122.7 in FY2026E, US$117.4 in FY2027E and US$113.6 in FY2028E, with the ore leg per tonne held roughly constant [S3]. One flat ratio would have grown processing revenue with limonite volume, which no guidance supports.

The earnings base we work from required one repair, which stands. The data pack carries a depreciation charge of about one dollar a year, two orders of magnitude below the audited segment note, which shows consolidated depreciation and amortisation of 90.9 USD m in FY2025A and 86.6 USD m in FY2024A [S2]. Restoring the audited charge takes FY2025A EBITDA to US$222.1m, a margin of 15.5% against 9.0% in FY2024A, and it is that restatement, not a forecast, which makes the cash-flow line and the DCF meaningful [S2].

Our forecast is the executed reality carried forward, not a normalisation. FY2026E revenue is US$2,699.4m, up 88.2%, on 22,000 thousand wet tonnes sold and a realised price of US$122.7 per wet tonne, which embeds the revised benchmark at a realisation ratio the assumption file sets at well under one per cent of the nickel price against a deck of 17,089.2 USD/t [S3]. EBITDA reaches US$497.8m at a 18.4% margin, then US$452.0m in FY2027E and US$396.2m in FY2028E as volume steps up, the margin drifting down as the processing block dilutes against more limonite tonnes [S3]. Volume reaches 25,000 thousand wet tonnes, the top of the guided range, and is then held flat because the mine's limonite reserve bounds the cumulative draw and the annual RKAB quota bounds each year's [S2].

Cash conversion is the weak link in the near term. Capex of US$253.0m, or US$11.5 per wet tonne sold, is above the US$193.3m of FY2025A because the leach circuits are still being completed, and working capital absorbs US$340.0m as receivables and stock scale with ore sales at 26.9% of revenue, so free cash flow to the firm is US$-136.9m in the first forecast year before recovering to US$108.7m and US$74.3m [S2]. From FY2029E capex steps down to US$5.4 per wet tonne, the reinvestment a depleting mine needs to stay whole, which is what turns the free cash flow line positive through the rest of the life [S2][S3]. The early-year deficit is a working-capital effect as much as an earnings effect, and it means the DCF value is unusually sensitive to the first three years.

The balance sheet is serviceable rather than strong. Net debt was US$752.3m at the FY2025A close and US$955.9m at FY2026E, or 1.9 times EBITDA, after US$355.0m of net borrowing to complete the acid-leach circuits [S2][S3]. Gross debt of US$944.9m is long-dated project debt carrying a marginal cost near 8.5%, and the interest line of 20.7 USD m in FY2025A is covered several times by EBITDA on the restated base [S2]. Leverage peaks at FY2028E, at US$952.0m or 2.4 times EBITDA, because the growth capex and the working-capital build front-run the cash recovery; it falls thereafter as capex steps down, so the placement is capital strengthening rather than a rescue [S2][S7].

Capital allocation is the largest governance question in the numbers. Dividends were US$0.0000 per share in FY2025A at a payout ratio of 0.0%, and every discretionary dollar has gone into the battery chain [S2]. Minority shareholders in the mine and the smelters take the bulk of the profit: consolidated net profit of US$270.4m yields US$79.5m attributable to the parent at a minority share of 70.6%, the FY2025 actual rather than a multi-year average because the mine is now the profit centre [S2][S0]. The private placement of up to 10,790,000,000 new shares, a dilution of about 10.0%, is modelled as dilution with the proceeds carried at cost in the bridge, because the price and the use of proceeds are still unset [S7].

Three earnings-quality flags deserve separate mention. First, the depreciation restatement above: any model that keeps the pack's charge overstates cash flow. Second, the intra-group ore sales, which are eliminated on consolidation and make reported mining revenue a poor guide to the group's external receipts [S3]. Third, the third-quarter collapse in processing margins, with the nickel pig iron cash cost printed at US$13,886/t Ni and the matte line at a negative cash margin, which tells us that the group's profit now depends on the mine and not on the converters [S3].

A nickel miner is a depleting asset with a policy-set price, so the method mix is the life-of-asset DCF, at 100%. We have removed the two multiples from the blend rather than re-weight them, and the review requires us to say why. The peer EV/EBITDA applied to trough FY2025A EBITDA of US$222.1m returns nothing for the equity once net debt and minorities are deducted, and a current-year multiple on a cyclical at the bottom of its price cycle is the procyclical error the house commodity card forbids [S2]. The price-to-book cross-check is worse than uninformative here: consolidated book is roughly half non-controlling interest and carries an asset revaluation, so a multiple of it would flatter the one method that appeared to corroborate the DCF [S2][S0]. A single method is disclosed as a single method; the sensitivity grid and the three scenarios are the cross-checks in its place.

The discount rate is built bottom-up. A risk-free rate of 4.9%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5% price the equity, with an unlevered beta of 1.10 levered to 1.70 at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.70 [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 16.3%. Pre-tax debt is priced in the engine at 6.9%, the USD risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread, and at weights of 59% equity and 41% debt the WACC is 11.8%. We flag one inconsistency we cannot fix inside the engine: the company's own debt stack prices at about 8.5%, and at this debt weight that would add roughly half a point to the WACC and take about a twentieth off the DCF, so the engine's rate is the more generous of the two and our target inherits that generosity rather than a harsher rate [S3].

Discounted at that rate, the life-of-asset cash flows are worth Rp39 per share, an enterprise value of US$1,614.5m. The terminal value share is 0%, because the horizon runs to reserve depletion and nothing is deferred into a growth perpetuity — for a single-mine producer that is a feature, not a limitation [S2]. The cash flows are back-loaded: the first forecast year contributes a small slice of present value after the working-capital build, and the second and third forecast years carry most of the total.
The bridge from enterprise to equity is where this report differs most from the initiation. Against an enterprise value of US$1,614.5m the bridge set out in

deducts net debt taken from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, deducts book non-controlling interests, adds associates and adds the placement item at cost and weighted for the probability that the shareholder meeting approves it, which is why the per-share value is a fraction of the enterprise value per share [S0][S7]. The bridge runs off the last reported balance sheet, not the FY2026E forecast; the forecast net debt and minority lines are described where they belong, in the financial analysis section [S0]. The mine that generates the group's profit is held indirectly and only half-owned, the conversion assets are partly owned, and the debt is consolidated in full. A reader who values consolidated EBITDA and forgets the minority claim will overstate the equity several times over.

The minority deduction needs a reconciliation, because it is the single largest item between the enterprise value and our target. The non-controlling interest deducted in the bridge is book value, and it is larger than the 70.6% profit share applied to the DCF's equity, so the base case deducts more for minorities than their cash-flow share alone would justify [S2][S0]. We disclose that as conservatism and do not correct it: the minority balance also carries the smelters' revalued assets, whose cash flows are inside this DCF, and the honest treatment of a claim we cannot buy out is its book value rather than a discount to it. The deduction therefore lowers the base case; it is not what carries the target. What lifts the probability-weighted target above the base case is the bull branch, worth Rp889 at a weight of 25%, and that weighting is why we rate REDUCE rather than a stronger sell.

We do not use the first sensitivity grid as evidence. Its price axis is an engine override that writes its forecast years back into the nickel deck, so in every cell the post-explicit price path stops escalating and the whole grid is computed on a lower path than the base case [S3]. The direction it shows is right, because the ore price is a ratio to the benchmark while the cost base is fixed in dollars, and the DCF is convex in it; the magnitude is not usable, and we have escalated the behaviour rather than quietened it, because an engine fix is outside an analyst's remit and a corrected grid would be a different report. The second grid, on volume and cost intensity, is faithful: a tenth of cost intensity costs the value about a tenth, and a tenth of volume rather less, because volume carries a working-capital cost as well as a revenue benefit. The asymmetry between the two concerns is the whole investment case in one picture: the ore price is what matters, the operating variables are second-order.

We do not quote a reverse DCF, and the reason is the same engine behaviour. The reverse solver targets the nickel deck, so it inherits the flattened post-explicit path and would report an implied ore price that is too low against our own base case; quoting it beside a target built on a tapering realisation would be incoherent, and we would rather disclose the gap than paper over it [S3]. What the price implies, stated without a solver, is an ore margin materially above the one the model delivers: at Rp312 the market is capitalising the enterprise well above the life-of-asset DCF, which is defensible only if the revised benchmark holds at the top of its range and the royalty take falls rather than rises [S3].

On the blend the base case is worth Rp39 today, and rolling that forward twelve months at the cost of equity gives Rp46. Probability-weighting the three scenario values gives the Rp245 target, which is -21.4% against the Rp312 price and the basis for our REDUCE rating. We state plainly how that target is carried: the base case alone is worth far less than the price, and the weighted value is lifted by the bull case, because the equity is a levered call on the ore price and the upper tail survives even after the royalty and the reserve life are charged against it [S3]. The target is expressed in rupiah and carries no liquidity discount [S0].

The risks that matter are the ones that move the ore price, and they are mostly regulatory. The revised Harga Patokan Mineral formula of 15 April and 15 September 2026 is the source of the entire earnings uplift, and a further revision that moved the reference back toward the old basis would take the mining margin with it [S3]. We carry that in the bear case rather than the base because the company treats the September revision as the settled framework, and because the royalty and tax take gives the government a direct interest in a higher reference [S3]. Likelihood we would put at low in any single year, impact severe: the mining segment is now the profit centre.

Nickel price risk is the largest market exposure. The house deck rises from 17,089.2 USD/t in FY2026E to 17,500.0 USD/t in FY2027E and escalates with US inflation thereafter, and the bear case marks the realised ore price down materially against that path [S3]. The mechanism is not subtle: the realised ore price is a fixed ratio to the benchmark, so a tenth off nickel is roughly a tenth off revenue and considerably more than a tenth off profit at current operating leverage. Demand risk is indirect, through Indonesian processing utilisation and RKAB quotas, rather than through a visible collapse in stainless or battery demand [S3].

Reserve and permitting risk are new to this revision and not second-order. The limonite reserve of 182,400 kt wmt proven plus 255,300 kt wmt probable ends the mine inside the DCF horizon; the saprolite reserve that feeds the smelters is smaller again at 34,500 kt wmt plus 106,700 kt wmt, and at the current quarter's delivery rate it is exhausted well before the limonite [S2][S3]. Separately, the company's targets are subject to RKAB approval and no archived source states the approved tonnage beyond the current year, so the volume path to the top of the guided range is unverified [S2].

Operational risk concentrates in the acid-leach ramp and in the cost line. The PT ESG lines were near nameplate at the end of the third quarter and the SLNC plant holds its industrial licence with first production targeted this year, but a commissioning delay pushes mixed hydroxide revenue to the right without touching the ore business [S3]. Cost risk is the one we take most seriously after the ore price, because fuel, hauling and royalties all rose together through 2026 and the residual cost block is the largest single input in the model [S2][S3].

Financial and governance risks are dilution and leakage. The private placement of up to 10,790,000,000 new shares, to be voted on 8 December 2026, adds about 10.0% to the register at a price that is not yet set, and we model it as dilution only [S7]. Minorities take 70.6% of consolidated profit, so a dollar of group profit is worth less than a third of a dollar to the listed equity [S2]. Related-party ore sales to group smelters are eliminated on consolidation, which limits the scope for transfer pricing but also obscures the true external realisable price [S3]. Liquidity is not a constraint: average daily traded value is well above the house threshold and no discount applies [S0].

The three cases carry probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25%, and they shock the same three drivers: the ore realisation, volume and the residual unit cost. The bear shocks the realisation by more than the bull lifts it, because the bear carries both a nickel price below the deck and a partial rollback of the revised formula, while no archived source supports a further re-rating above the formula already deployed; the asymmetry is disclosed rather than hidden [S3]. The bear case is worth Rp0 per share, the base case Rp46 and the bull case Rp889. The distribution is wide because the DCF is convex in the ore price: the downside case loses the equity value while the upside case multiplies it, even though the underlying shocks are modest.

Four signposts would change our view. A further revision to the ore benchmark formula that lowers the reference would move us toward the bear case immediately. A 2027 RKAB quota below the 2026 level would do the same through volume. A quarter of limonite sales below the run-rate needed to reach the low end of guidance would tell us the ramp is demand-constrained rather than mine-constrained [S3]. And a second consecutive quarter of negative cash margin in matte, or a nickel pig iron cash cost above the current level, would confirm that processing is a permanent drag rather than a cyclical trough [S3].

Merdeka Battery Materials is controlled but not a family conglomerate in the house sense. PT Merdeka Energi Nusantara, a subsidiary of the listed Merdeka Copper Gold group, holds half the register, the public holds roughly a third, and two industrial shareholders hold stakes above the disclosure threshold [S2]. The free float of 26.5% clears the exchange minimum but is thin, and the model applies no liquidity discount because traded value is high [S0]. The practical consequence is that minority holders have little blocking power over related-party or capital-raising resolutions.

The board is professional rather than founder-led, and cross-directorships with the parent are disclosed in the annual report [S2][S0]. The accounts are audited by the Indonesian member firm of BDO, which most recently issued an unmodified opinion, and the audit relationship has been stable through the reporting period we rely on [S2]. We see no auditor or restatement red flag; the depreciation problem we corrected sits in the third-party data pack, not in the audited accounts, which is why we restated to them rather than around them [S2].

Related-party dealings are structural and disclosed. The company sells ore to smelters it partly owns, buys services from group entities, and processes pyrite from the parent's copper mine at its acid and iron circuit, so a meaningful share of reported revenue and cost is internal and eliminated on consolidation [S2]. That reduces the risk of value leaking through uneconomic third-party contracts but makes the external realised price harder to observe, and it is the main reason we anchor the valuation on the consolidated revenue-per-tonne ratio rather than on the mining segment's reported price [S3].

The dividend record is empty. No dividend has been paid and the payout ratio is set at 0.0% in our forecast, which is consistent with a company still building processing capacity [S2]. The company has raised capital rather than returned it: the placement of up to 10,790,000,000 new shares was announced with a capital-strengthening rationale, and the extraordinary general meeting is set for 8 December 2026 [S7][S8]. The dilution is modelled, but the terms are not disclosed, which is a governance gap as much as a valuation one.

ESG exposure is concentrated in the ore-to-chemicals chain. The company holds reclamation and mine-closure provisions and reports rehabilitation, mangrove planting and a recycling programme through a subsidiary, together with an energy policy adopted in 2025 [S2]. The emissions-intensive parts of the chain are the kilns and the hauling fleet, and the President Director's report identifies higher royalty, fuel and hauling costs as the cost pressures of the year, so a carbon cost or a fuel-supply shock would land directly on the unit cost line we model [S2][S3]. Battery-chain customers impose responsible-sourcing and emissions measurement requirements on suppliers, which is a commercial risk for the mixed hydroxide product rather than a compliance one at this stage [S2].

The calendar is short and dominated by corporate events. The extraordinary general meeting on 8 December 2026 votes on the placement of up to 10,790,000,000 new shares and the capital increase [S7][S8]. The full-year results in the first quarter of 2027 carry the first clean read on the revised ore benchmark across a full year and the 2027 guidance [S3]. The annual RKAB quota decision in the second quarter is the main supply lever behind the nickel price the model carries, and the SLNC plant's first mixed hydroxide precipitate is targeted before the end of this year [S3][S2].

Between updates we monitor a short list. Ore production and, more importantly, ore sold, because the company can draw on stockpiles and a production record is not the same as a sales record [S3]. The realised limonite and saprolite prices against the Harga Patokan Mineral reference, which is where the policy pass-through shows first [S3]. Nickel pig iron and matte cash costs per tonne, because a second quarter of negative matte margin would confirm that the converters are a permanent drag [S3]. High-pressure acid leach utilisation and acid plant output, as the leading indicators for the battery-chain revenue that sits inside our revenue-per-tonne ratio [S3]. Net debt and the placement terms, which determine whether the equity story is dilution-funded growth or balance-sheet repair [S7].

Two monitoring items are not in the company's control and matter more than any of the above. The first is the ore benchmark formula itself: the September 2026 revision is the reason our earnings base is what it is, and any further revision is the single largest swing factor in the model [S3]. The second is the Indonesian supply discipline that sets the nickel deck, which we hold at house values but which the bear case discounts materially over the life of the asset [S3].

bear.narrative: Indonesian supply discipline fails and the nickel deck runs about 15% too high; the revised HPM formula is partly rolled back so the ore realisation falls to about two thirds of the deployed ratio, which carries both the price shock and the mirror of the 2026 windfall the thesis rests on; ore volumes come in 5% under plan as RKAB quotas and wet-season haulage bind; and the unit cash-cost residual runs 10% above plan on fuel and royalties. The price shock is carried on the realisation ratio rather than on the deck multiplier because the engine's deck override writes its forecast years back into the deck and flattens the post-FY2030 price path, understating every override run.

bull.narrative: Indonesia enforces the ore-trading crackdown and cuts 2027 RKAB quotas, tightening nickel supply so the benchmark and the ore realisation run 15% above the base; ore volumes come in 5% above plan as the SCM quota is renewed higher and the HPAL lines pull more limonite; and the unit cash-cost residual eases 10% on fuel and hauling efficiency. No further HPM re-rating is assumed beyond the price linkage already deployed, so the bull does not double count the 2026 step.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: Limonite ore sold, in kt wmt. FY2025A was 16.8m wmt (F3/S2 p.118). 2026 guidance is 20.0-25.0m wmt of limonite sales (S3 p.2) and nine months of 2026 already delivered 15.7m wmt (1Q26 4.8m, 2Q26 3.3m, 3Q26 7.6m, S3 p.3 Table 1), so FY2026E is set at 22.0m wmt — the low half of the guided range, with a fourth quarter at roughly the 3Q26 rate and not the guided ceiling. FY2027E rises to 24.0m wmt and FY2028E-FY2030E to 25.0m wmt, the top of the current guidance range, as the PT ESG HPAL lines run at nameplate and SLNC starts MHP production (S3 p.1); no source supports sales above the guided ceiling, so the model does not assume one. Held flat in real terms after FY2028E.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: This is a REVENUE-PER-TONNE BRIDGE, not a price discount. The denominator is the LME/HPM nickel benchmark in USD per tonne of contained metal (deck FY2026E 17,089.25); the numerator is total consolidated revenue per limonite wmt sold. FY2025A: revenue 1,434.5m (F7/S2 p.131) over 16.8m wmt sold (F3) is 85.4 USD/wmt, 0.00563 of the FY2025 benchmark (15,162). FY2026E: nine months of 2026 ran at roughly 2.0bn of consolidated sales (built from the quarterly NPI, HGNM, limonite, saprolite and acid lines in S3 p.3 and the 3Q26 sales table, S3 p.18: total 726.7m in the quarter alone) on 15.7m wmt, and a fourth quarter at the 3Q run-rate puts FY2026E revenue near 2.70bn, or 123 USD/wmt — 0.00718 of the FY2026E benchmark. The step up from FY2025 is the revised Mineral Benchmark Price formula, which took effect on 15 April 2026 and again on 15 September 2026 and lifted 3Q26 limonite ASP 68% YoY to 24.2 USD/wmt and saprolite ASP 169% to 66.8 USD/wmt (S3 p.1, p.4-p.5; F21-F22). The ratio then TAPERS as the denominator grows, because only the ore leg scales with limonite volume: 3Q26 non-limonite revenue was 542.1m of the 726.7m total on 7.6m wmt, or 71.3 USD per limonite wmt (S3 p.18), while processing revenue is guided flat at 70,000-80,000 tNi of NPI and 44,000-48,000 t of HGNM (S3 p.2). Lifting limonite sales from 22.0m to 25.0m wmt therefore leaves total revenue per wet tonne lower, not higher: 0.00718 in FY2026E (22.0m wmt), 0.00671 in FY2027E (24.0m) and 0.00649 from FY2028E (25.0m), which holds the ore leg per tonne constant and lets the flat processing block dilute. Because the ratio is calibrated on the FY2026E run-rate rather than on FY2025A, the engine's FY2025A re-pricing test shows a gap of about minus 6.5 per cent (modelled EBITDA 207.7 against the reported 222.1, S2): the pre-HPM FY2025A base is being re-priced with the FY2026E ratio, and the shortfall is the April and September 2026 formula revision not yet being in the FY2025A revenue line, not a model error. The FY2025A test is therefore a basis check, not a forecast.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: there is no administered price ceiling on nickel ore. The HPM is a government benchmark used to set royalty and tax, and the revised formula lifted ore prices rather than capping them (S3 p.1); no domestic-market obligation applies to nickel ore.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 as a cost-intensity factor, not a physical strip ratio. MBMA does not disclose a waste-to-ore ratio in the archived record; the annual report gives cash cost per wmt instead (limonite 10.0 USD/wmt in 2025, F16/S2 p.47), so the template's strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm term is kept as a per-tonne mining cost with no unsourced creep.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: US$12.3 per wmt, the last actual: limonite cash cost (ex-royalty) was 12.3 USD/wmt in 3Q26 and about 12.4 across the nine months, against 10.0 in FY2025 and 10.1 in 1Q26 (F32/S3 p.3 Table 1). The house rule is costs at the last actual in real terms, and the last actual is 12.3, not the 10.0 of 2025; the company is "maintaining guidance but closely monitoring fuel price and consumption" with limonite cash costs below US$11/wmt (S3 p.2), so the gap to guidance is disclosed and held in the company's favour only where the record supports it, which here it does not. With the intensity factor at 1.0 this is the mining component of the unit cost. It is escalated with the coal deck only through the fuel term.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Left at the 30% engine constant. MBMA does not disclose the diesel share of the SCM mine cost, and the annual report flags fuel price and consumption as the cost variable the company is monitoring in its 2026 guidance (S3 p.2). Mining is open-pit haulage, so a fuel linkage is right in direction; the size is the engine default rather than a sourced figure, and it applies only to the US$10.0/wmt mining term, not to the processing residual.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: US$71.4 per limonite wmt: hauling, barging, and the smelting/refining conversion costs (RKEF, HGNM matte, HPAL) that sit in cost of revenue but are not captured in the mining term. Backed out of the accounts rather than disclosed: FY2025 cost of revenue was 1,268.0m (F9/S2 p.131) less royalty 52.7m (F13) less the depreciation inside cost of revenue (~86.5m of the 90.9m total, F5) is 1,128.8m of cash cost on 16.8m wmt, i.e. 67.2 USD/wmt. The 2026 cost base is higher per wmt because the matte plant and the AIM acid plant are now running and 3Q26 limonite cash cost rose to 12.3 USD/wmt and saprolite to 31.0 USD/wmt on higher royalties, fuel and hauling (S3 p.4-p.5); the FY2026E level is calibrated so that revenue, royalty, opex and this cost reproduce the 3Q26 consolidated cash margin run-rate. Held flat in real terms.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: 9.30% of revenue, the effective rate the last actual quarter shows. The royalty base is ore value at the Harga Patokan Mineral, not group revenue, so it rose with the revised benchmark even though processing revenue did not: 3Q26 royalty was 5.3 USD/wmt on limonite and 9.4 on saprolite (F30, F31/S3 p.3 Table 1), 40.3m plus 27.3m on the quarter's sales, or 67.6m against the 726.7m of consolidated revenue reported for the quarter (S3 p.18) — 9.3 per cent. The FY2025 charge was 3.68% of revenue (52.73m on 1,434.52m, F13/S2 note 26) because ore prices were then below the new reference; carrying that rate into FY2026E would understate the royalty by roughly 5.6 points of revenue. The rate is held flat on revenue after FY2026E and is a proxy: it moves with the ore-price leg, which is the leg that scales with the nickel deck inside this single-denominator model.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Zero: the single-denominator build already carries every revenue stream (ore, NPI, matte, acid, LGNM) inside the revenue-per-limonite-wmt ratio, so a second block would double count. The 3Q26 sales table shows the streams and sums to total consolidated sales of 726.7m in the quarter (S3 p.18).

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Not used: other revenue is zero in every forecast year, so this margin has no effect on the model. Left at the engine constant rather than given an invented basis.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: US$5.41 per limonite wmt: consolidated depreciation and amortisation of 90.89m in FY2025 (F5/S2 segment note; the data pack's 1.0m is the direct-method cash-flow artefact the accounts do not show, and the LK 90.89m is the real charge) over 16.8m wmt sold (F3). The FY2024 charge was 86.61m (F6), consistent at ~7.9 USD/wmt on 11.0m wmt, so the ratio moves with the asset base rather than with the mining volume alone; holding the FY2025 level is the neutral choice given the matte plant and the acid plant are now in service. The engine restates FY2024A and FY2025A D&A from these facts.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: US$11.5 per limonite wmt for FY2026E-FY2028E, the FY2025 actual level: the annual report records a 2025 capital expenditure budget of 210.4m and actual investment of 192.8m, mostly AIM I and SCM mine infrastructure (S2 p.137-p.139), against 16.8m wmt sold (F3). That spend is growth capex, not sustaining, so it is held only through the build years and then steps down to US$5.41 per wmt from FY2029E — the FY2025 D&A per wet tonne (F5/S2 over F3), the reinvestment that keeps a depleting mine whole with no growth and no decay. The expansion capex is not double counted: the December 2026 placement and the FPP/HPAL spend it funds are carried at cost as a bridge item. Holding the 2025 build rate for the whole life charged 63% of EBITDA to capex and would have valued the ore body at less than its debt.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the HPAL and feed-preparation spend is inside the capex intensity above (the 2025 budget was mostly AIM I and mine infrastructure, S2 p.137), and no archived source gives a project value for the 55,000 tonne MHP HPAL/FPP that the placement is meant to fund (S7). Capitalising an unsourced project number would put a typed figure into the model.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 26.9% of revenue, the FY2025 actual: operating working capital of 385.58m on revenue of 1,434.52m (S0 pack). The pack default of 17.2% is a three-year average dragged down by FY2022A, when the mine was ramping and revenue was a third of today's; the last actual ratio is the right anchor for a business whose receivables and inventory now scale with a much larger ore and smelter book. Held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 11%, the FY2025 actual effective rate: tax of 12.04m on pre-tax profit of 112.56m (S0 pack), consistent with FY2024's 10.6% and with the tax holidays and allowances the smelter subsidiaries carry. Held flat; the statutory 22% is not the effective charge.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.5%, set from the debt stack disclosed at 30 September 2026 rather than from the pack's 3.0% historical average: IDR bonds of 822m equivalent carrying 9.00%-10.50% coupons, IDR sukuk of 176m, and the 100m Facility A plus 92m Facility B drawn (S3 p.17-p.18). The 3.0% default is the FY2023-FY2025 average, before the bond programme scaled up, and would understate interest by more than half.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 2.8%: FY2025 interest income of 6.86m (F12/S2 p.131) over opening cash of 244.03m (S0 pack). Close to a USD deposit rate on a working balance that is drawn down through the year.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: 355m in FY2026E, zero afterwards. The pack's FY2025 closing debt was 944.94m and the 30 June 2026 balance was 1,300.32m (S0 pack latest_bs); the 30 September 2026 stack (IDR bonds 822m, sukuk 176m, Facility A 100m, Facility B 92m, S3 p.17-p.18) is of the same order. The step keeps the interest line on the debt actually outstanding, after which free cash flow repays rather than adds debt because no new facility is announced in the record.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating item is disclosed. The FY2025 accounts carry a finance cost line already modelled through debt (F11) and no separately recurring associate or one-off line is large enough to forecast.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 70.6%, the FY2025A actual: net profit was 100.51m against 29.56m attributable to parent (S0). It is high because the SCM mine, the group's profit centre, is only 51% owned — MBMA holds it indirectly through its 95.3% acquisition of MIN — and the RKEF and matte smelters are partly owned too (S2 p.176 ownership note). The model uses the last audited split rather than the pack's three-year average, because the 2026 mix puts a larger share of group profit in the mine. The DCF's equity bridge deducts the minority claim on the value of the business separately (see valuation.bridge); this input drives the reported attributable profit line only.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company has never paid a dividend. The pack carries dps of zero for every year from FY2023A to FY2025A and no dividend is proposed in the archived record (S0, S7, S8); the 2026 private placement is explicitly to strengthen capital, not to distribute it (S7). No payout is assumed in the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Plus 10% in FY2027E, zero in the other years. The company will ask shareholders on 8 December 2026 to approve a private placement of up to 10.79bn new shares with a stated paid-in capital increase of "maksimal 10%" (F23/S7; S8), which on 107.99bn shares outstanding (S0) is roughly a tenth of the register. Because the EGM and pricing are not complete, the dilution is placed in the first full year after approval rather than in FY2026E.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.0%, the house terminal growth for a USD reporting currency. It enters only the cross-check DCF with a terminal value; the primary valuation is the life-of-asset DCF, which has no terminal value and ends with the reserves.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 2.46% of revenue, the FY2025 actual: SG&A and other operating expense of 35.53m on revenue of 1,434.52m (S0 pack). The pack default of 2.21% is the three-year average including FY2022A, when revenue was a third of the current base and the ratio was flattered. Held flat; a corporate cost base that grows with the smelter book is already inside the ratio.

challenges.challenge: Any override on d.metals.nickel silently flattens the price path. A 1.0x multiplier is a no-op by construction, yet the sensitivity grid's centre prints Rp258 against the base's Rp471 (v0 222.3 vs 404.8): _apply_overrides writes each year's resolved deck value back into values, and deck_value derives post-explicit years from the latest written explicit year, so FY2030E-FY2050E all receive 17,500 x 1.02 (about 17,850, ASP about 128.2) instead of escalating to about 26,500 (ASP 190.4). The bear (85), bull (989), every sensitivity cell and the reverse DCF therefore run on a different, much lower path than the base they are blended with, and the Rp504 target mixes two bases.
challenges.answer: Accepted as engine behaviour I cannot fix from the analyst seat: _apply_overrides writes shocked deck values back into node values, so post-explicit years stop escalating. Scenario price shocks now run through a.realisation, which never touches the deck; the report quotes no grid centre, no reverse DCF and no sensitivity magnitude, and the behaviour is escalated to the Sector Lead and OPS.

challenges.challenge: The summary and section 4 say the reverse DCF returns 17,832 USD/t, 2% above the deck's anchor and 9% above spot, and conclude the equity already capitalises the house price deck and not the ore margin. On the base deck the life-of-asset DCF is Rp552 and the 12-month value Rp471 against a Rp312 price, so a reverse solve must return a nickel price materially BELOW 17,500 (of the order of spot), not above it. The 17,832 is reproducible only on the flattened deck of C1. The central claim is inverted.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF was inverted because it solved on the flattened deck of C1. It is removed from the summary and section 4; the report now states what the price implies without a solver and says plainly why no reverse is quoted [S3].

challenges.challenge: Royalty is held at 3.68% of group revenue, the FY2025 effective rate. The royalty base is ore value, not group revenue: 3Q26 royalty was 5.3 USD/wmt on limonite and 9.4 on saprolite (S3 p.3-4), about 67.5m in the quarter, or 9.3% of 726.7m of revenue (5.5% on the external limonite line alone). The assumption's defence - that the rise is the ad valorem rate on a higher HPM price which the revenue line already carries - is wrong in direction, because processing revenue does not rise with the ore price. On FY2026E revenue this omits roughly 50-150m a year, 7-21% of EBITDA, in a DCF levered about five times to EBITDA.
challenges.answer: Royalty rebuilt on ore value: 9.3 per cent of consolidated revenue from 5.3 USD/wmt on limonite and 9.4 on saprolite in 3Q26, against 3.68 per cent of FY2025 revenue [S3, S2]. Every forecast year and the long run are reset, and the report says why processing revenue does not rise with the ore price.

challenges.challenge: The DCF is sold as running to reserve depletion but mines 621m wmt of limonite (22 + 24 + 23 x 25 for FY2026-FY2050) against limonite reserves of 437.7m wmt (AR 2025 Table 2: 182.4 proven plus 255.3 probable wet tonnes); the 578.8m wmt in fact F4 is the total for both ore types and includes 141.2m wmt of saprolite. Limonite depletes around FY2043, so about 15% of the EV (roughly Rp80/share) sits in FY2044-FY2050 with no ore, and the saprolite revenue inside the ratio is drawn from a reserve the 3Q26 run-rate (3.3m wmt a quarter) exhausts in about 11 years.
challenges.answer: The horizon is now limonite depletion, 17 years drawing 421m of the 437.7m wmt limonite reserve [S2]. Facts F26 to F29 split proven and probable by ore type, F4 is relabelled as the total for both ore types, and the saprolite reserve is disclosed as the smelter feed constraint.

challenges.challenge: EV/EBITDA carries 25% weight at the 5.96x peer median on trough FY2025A EBITDA of 222.1m and returns Rp0, dragging the blend from the DCF's Rp552 to Rp405 - 27% of the target. House card step 1 forbids valuing a cyclical on current-year multiples (procyclical error #1), and the November CHEMICALS review fixed exactly this error in APLI by moving to a 100% DCF target. A method that returns zero because its denominator precedes the re-pricing cannot be a 25% cross-check.
challenges.answer: Weights moved to 100 per cent life-of-asset DCF. The trough-year EV/EBITDA and the P/BV on revalued half-minority book are removed rather than re-weighted, and section 4 states the procyclical objection and that a single method is disclosed as such [S2, S0].

challenges.challenge: Unit costs are anchored on FY2025: cost_per_bcm 10.0/wmt (F16) and other_cost_unit 71.4 backed out of FY2025 cost of revenue. The only 2026 actuals are worse: limonite cash cost 12.3/wmt in 3Q26 and about 12.4 across 9M (S3 p.3), above the 'below 11' guidance the company is 'maintaining but closely monitoring'; NPI cash cost is up 53% YoY to 13,886/tNi and HGNM 16,734/tNi on a negative cash margin. The house rule is costs at the last actual, and the last actual is 12.3, not 10.0. The gap is about 50m a year, 7% of EBITDA, in every forecast year.
challenges.answer: Mining cost reset to the last actual, 12.3 USD/wmt 3Q26 limonite cash cost, in every forecast year and the long run, replacing the FY2025 10.0 [S3]. The report discloses that guidance below the old level is no longer being met.

challenges.challenge: SLNC's 90,000 tpa MHP plant completed commissioning in 3Q26 with first ore feed at end-September (S3 p.10), and PT ESG produced 9,742 t of nickel in MHP at 96% utilisation with a 27,000-30,000 t target; the model assigns them nothing - capex_other is zero and the flat revenue-per-limonite-wmt ratio has no volume or margin for a new external stream. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires a development project to be carried at least at sourced sunk capex, never zero.
challenges.answer: The placement-funded feed-preparation plant and HPAL spend are carried in the equity bridge at cost and probability-weighted, per the development-project rule, and the SLNC and PT ESG ramp is described in section 1 [S7, S3].

challenges.challenge: The 10.79bn-share placement (about 10% dilution, EGM 8 December 2026) is modelled as dilution with no proceeds because price and use of proceeds are unset. The shares are not a gift: at Rp312 they raise about Rp3.4tr, roughly 184m USD or Rp30/share, and the FY2026E plan also adds 355m of net borrowing to fund the build. Modelling the dilution and not the cash is a one-sided treatment of a post-balance-sheet event the house card puts in the bridge.
challenges.answer: The placement proceeds are in the bridge at the current Rp312 price, 184m at cost and weighted 0.85 for the shareholder vote, so dilution and cash are treated on the same basis [S7, S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear case shocks nickel, volume and cost and leaves the HPM ore realisation untouched, so the one driver that produces the entire call has no downside scenario, although the government re-wrote the formula twice in six months (15 April and 15 September 2026) and the base assumes the September version persists for 25 years at a fixed 0.00718 ratio to LME. A reversal of the 2026 uplift - the mirror of the windfall the thesis relies on - is absent from the bear, the grid and the reverse.
challenges.answer: The bear now shocks the ore realisation to 0.68 of the base path, mirrored by a 1.15 bull, and the probability stays at 0.25. The narrative carries both a nickel price below the deck and a partial rollback of the revised formula, and section 5 states the asymmetry instead of calling the shocks symmetric [S3].

challenges.challenge: RKAB quota risk is named but not sized. Limonite sales are raised to 25m wmt, the top of the 2026 guidance range, and held for 23 years on an annual permit, while the government is publicly preparing production restrictions through RKAB (news, 4 November 2026) and nickel trades near 15,800 on oversupply. A quota-constrained volume is the likeliest path if the supply discipline the bull case wants actually happens, and it is not modelled.
challenges.answer: Volume is capped at the top of the 2026 guidance range and inside the limonite reserve, and the RKAB exposure is disclosed rather than sized because no archived source states the approved tonnage beyond the current year [S2, S4]. Section 2 and section 5 say so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The single ratio cannot separate ore from processing. Non-limonite revenue per limonite wmt was about 71 in 3Q26 (726.7m less 184.6m limonite over 7.6m wmt) but about 135 in 1H26, because the denominator is quarterly limonite sales, which swung from 3.3m to 7.6m wmt. Carrying one annual ratio to 25m wmt while NPI is guided flat at 70,000-80,000 tNi and HGNM at 44,000-48,000 t implicitly grows processing revenue per limonite tonne by about 14%, or else credits an SLNC/acid ramp the report values at zero elsewhere.
challenges.answer: The realisation now tapers as the limonite denominator grows, 0.00718 in FY2026E to 0.00649 from FY2028E and in the long run, because processing revenue is guided flat on NPI and HGNM. Section 3 shows the revenue per wet tonne falling year by year [S3].

challenges.challenge: Cost of capital inputs conflict. Section 4 states a pre-tax debt cost of 6.9% and the WACC uses kd_pre_tax 6.86% (engine default: risk-free plus a zero spread), while a.cost_of_debt is 8.5% from the 30 September 2026 stack the analyst sourced (IDR bonds 9.00-10.50%, sukuk, facilities). At the 41% debt weight the gap is about 0.5pp of WACC and 5-6% of the DCF, and the report's own basis and prose disagree.
challenges.answer: The engine has no kd input: it computes kd as the USD risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread, 6.9 per cent, and ignores a.cost_of_debt for the WACC, which I cannot change without editing the engine. The sourced 8.5 per cent stack is disclosed in section 4 with its effect, about half a point of WACC and a twentieth of the DCF, so the direction of the gap is stated against the target [S3, S0].

challenges.challenge: The equity bridge deducts book non-controlling interest of 840m (17% of the 4,814m EV) while the model books 73.7% of consolidated net profit (337m of 457.7m in FY2026E) to minorities - a 2.5x multiple on the minority earnings stream. If the upstream mine is largely wholly owned, as the HPM thesis implies, the P&L minority share is too high and np_parent of 120.3m is understated; if it is right, the bridge under-deducts by 1-2bn. The report asserts both.
challenges.answer: The minority share is now the FY2025A actual, 70.6 per cent of net profit, replacing the three-year average, and section 4 reconciles the book non-controlling interest deducted in the bridge with that profit share and states that the book deduction is the conservative side [S0, S2].

flags.message: a.capex_unit moves -57% in real terms from FY2026E to FY2042E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex steps down from 11.5 USD/wmt to 5.41 from FY2029E, a sourced real-terms change: 11.5 is the FY2025 build rate (192.8m actual on 16.8m wmt, F3, [S2] p.137) including AIM I growth capex, and 5.41 is the FY2025 depreciation and amortisation per wet tonne (F5 over F3), the reinvestment that holds a depleting mine whole. The expansion capex is not lost: the December 2026 placement and the FPP/HPAL spend it funds are carried at cost as a bridge item [S7].

flags.message: a.realisation: bear 0.68 vs bull 1.15 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: Bear and bull shock the same three drivers — the ore realisation, volume and the unit cost residual. The bull shocks them 1.15x, 1.05x and 0.9x; the bear 0.68x, 0.95x and 1.1x. The bear's realisation multiplier carries both a nickel price about 15 per cent below the deck and a partial rollback of the revised Harga Patokan Mineral formula toward the FY2025 ratio (0.00563 against 0.00718; F14, F21, F22 [S3]), which the government has already rewritten twice in six months, on 15 April and 15 September 2026 [S3] p.1. The asymmetry is sourced: there is a live policy-reversal risk on the downside and no archived source for a further re-rating above the deployed formula on the upside. Any shock on a deck variable would also trigger an engine behaviour that flattens the post-FY2030 price path, so the price shocks are carried on the realisation input, which is faithful to the deck.

flags.message: the price driver d.metals.nickel must be shocked in both cases
flags.justification: No scenario shocks the deck variable directly. Every override on a deck variable makes the engine write the shocked value back into the deck for every forecast year, so the post-FY2030 path stops escalating and every such run is measured against a lower price path than the base. The price shock therefore travels through a.realisation, the ratio of revenue per wet tonne to the benchmark, which multiplies the untouched deck: 0.68x in the bear and 1.15x in the bull, with the volume and unit-cost shocks mirrored around 1.0 as in the industry default [S3]. That is an engine limitation escalated to the Sector Lead, not a modelling choice.

flags.message: the DCF stops after 17 years while reserves last ~26 years at FY+1 volume: extend the horizon or justify the cut
flags.justification: The 17-year cut is the limonite reserve, not a caution: the DCF volume is limonite ore sold and the mine's limonite reserve is 182.4m wmt proven plus 255.3m wmt probable, 437.7m wmt (F26, F27/S2 p.26 Table 2), while the 578.8m wmt the check uses is the total for both ore types and includes 141.2m wmt of saprolite (F28, F29/S2 p.26). The path draws 421.0m wmt of limonite over 17 years, leaving 16.7m wmt in the ground, so a longer horizon would mine ore the reserve statement does not support.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_life': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pbv': 0.15}
flags.justification: The target is 100 per cent life-of-asset DCF because a nickel miner at the bottom of a price cycle cannot be valued on a current-year multiple: the peer-median EV/EBITDA applied to trough FY2025A EBITDA of 222m against net debt plus minorities returns zero equity, and the P/BV of 1.78x is struck on consolidated book that is half non-controlling interest and carries a PSAK 16 revaluation [S2][S0]. The CHEMICALS review settled the same point for APLI by moving that name to a 100% DCF target.
